## TL;DR

Fixed Review 11's merge-drift classification. Merge commits are now compared with the check-start tree, so an older source commit on a side branch is not treated as new drift when its content was already present at check start and the merge only adds bookkeeping. Ordinary first-parent commits remain inspected individually, preserving detection of a source change followed by a revert. The focused bookkeeping suite passed all 27 tests, and the final `repoos check --changed main` passed after the requested main merge.

## Work and rationale

The drift checker already limited traversal to the checked branch's first-parent timeline. It still compared each merge result to the merge's first parent, which could attribute source history from the merged branch to the task even when the resulting tree contained no new source content relative to the tree actually validated.

The checker now selects its comparison base by commit type. Ordinary commits compare against their first parent, retaining commit-level detection when source content changes and is later restored. Merge commits compare against the check-start commit. Git's tree diff compares resulting content, and the bookkeeping path filter then permits only `work/**` and `.repoos/**` changes. If the merge result contains a source change relative to the start tree, the merge subject and changed paths still invalidate the check. Unavailable ancestry or path information continues to fail closed.

The accepted source-write limitation remains documented: RepoOS refuses new managed engineer turns during a gate and detects committed source changes after the check, but an already-running engineer can write files directly. Those filesystem writes cannot be reliably fenced. This work does not try to block them.

## Approaches tried

I retained first-parent traversal instead of inspecting every newly reachable side-branch commit. Within that traversal, ordinary commits and merge commits need different comparisons. An ordinary commit needs its own parent delta so a source edit followed by a revert is still observed. A merge needs the net comparison against the start snapshot so equivalent source content from its side branch is not misclassified as new drift.

I changed the accepted merge fixture from an `ours` strategy merge to a normal merge. The side branch contains an older source change plus a bookkeeping file; the checked branch independently commits identical source content before the gate starts. The merge's net tree delta is only `work/side-report.md`, and the check accepts it. A companion fixture merges source content that differs from the start tree and checks that the result is rejected with the merge subject and source path. The existing source-change-then-revert fixture remains to verify individual ordinary commits are still checked.

## Challenges and blockers

The first run of the focused test caught a mismatched quote in the new merge assertion before any test executed. I corrected it, reran the focused suite, and all 27 tests passed. Formatting was applied with the repository formatter.

The owner requested bringing main into the branch because its task-file copy now documents the accepted scope. The merge preview showed a conflict only in this task's work file; I resolved it by taking main's copy, as instructed. I restored the branch's original `repoos.toml` content before creating the merge commit, leaving that file unchanged. I rebuilt after the merge, then ran the final scoped RepoOS check. Remote validation passed on the retry after the initial ThinkPad container timed out; local guards, rendered contrast, UI smoke and the user-docs build passed as well.

## Key learnings

Commit ancestry alone does not show whether a merge changed the checked source tree. Merge commits should be judged by their resulting content compared with the check-start snapshot, while ordinary commits should remain individually inspected when temporary source changes must invalidate a run. Test fixtures should use normal merges and assert actual net paths so they exercise the content the drift check relies on. Source-write documentation should describe the accepted after-the-fact detection boundary without claiming that an already-running process is fenced.
